extracted.intended_audience: researchers, NLP practitioners, and research funders interested in automated analysis of grant peer review reports
extracted.subtask_description: Develop and validate sentence-level annotations and transformer-based classifiers to identify substantive characteristics of grant peer review reports for funder-facing evaluation and research. The workflow covers codebook development, human annotation, model fine-tuning, evaluation, and explainability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Track Record and Expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the sentence address the scientific qualifications of the applicant(s)/team?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part of the Evaluation Criteria dimension. Example sentences include comments on applicants' expertise, publication record, or prior accomplishments (see Appendix F.1). This category is non-exclusive and can co-occur with other categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the sentence address the suitability of the methods to be used within the proposed research project?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part of the Evaluation Criteria dimension. Includes explicit judgments about whether chosen methods are appropriate or state-of-the-art (see Appendix F.3). Annotate at sentence level; category can co-occur with Methods and Feasibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance, Originality, and Topicality
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the sentence address the scientific relevance/originality/topicality of the proposed research project?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part of the Evaluation Criteria dimension. Captures statements about novelty, importance, and timeliness of the proposal (examples in Appendix F.2). Non-exclusive with other Evaluation Criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feasibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the sentence address the feasibility of the proposed research project?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part of the Evaluation Criteria dimension. Includes assessments of achievability given expertise, aims, timeline, and resources (examples in Appendix F.4). Feasibility often co-occurs with Suitability and Methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant: Quantity
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the sentence use quantitative indicators to describe the applicant(s) or team?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part of the Focus dimension. Captures explicit numeric or bibliometric mentions (e.g., publication counts, h-index, patents). This category is rare (1.6% in annotated sample) but distinct from qualitative Applicant comments (Appendix F.8).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposal
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the sentence address the proposal or specific parts of it, as opposed to the applicant(s) or context beyond the proposal?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part of the Focus dimension. Applies to sentences addressing the proposal content, rationale, structure, or scope (examples in Appendix F.5). Prevalent in annotations (~41%).

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the sentence address the applicant(s)/team or their qualifications, without mentioning quantitative indicators?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part of the Focus dimension. Includes qualitative judgments about the team's fit, expertise, or institutional affiliations (see Appendix F.7). Distinct from ‘Applicant: Quantity’ which captures numeric indicators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the sentence address the methods to be used in the proposed research project?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part of the Focus dimension. Captures discussion of methodological choices or appropriateness (Appendix F.6). Can overlap with Suitability and Feasibility categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Positive statement
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the sentence itself a positive statement or does it contain a positive statement?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part of the Statement Type and Reasoning dimension. Marks supportive or favorable assessments. Not all positive statements contain a Rationale; prevalence ~37.1% in the sample (examples in Appendix F.9).

rubrics_metrics.name: Suggestion
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the sentence suggest how to improve the proposal?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part of the Statement Type and Reasoning dimension. Captures actionable recommendations or requests for clarification (examples in Appendix F.12). Low prevalence (~4.5%).

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative statement
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the sentence itself a negative statement or does it contain a negative statement?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part of the Statement Type and Reasoning dimension. Marks critical or unfavorable assessments. Negative statements sometimes lack explicit Rationale (examples in Appendix F.10).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the sentence provide rational supporting the positive or negative statement?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part of the Statement Type and Reasoning dimension. Important: Rationale was only considered if the annotator first identified a positive or a negative statement. Rationale was the most challenging category (highest perceived difficulty and lowest F1). Examples in Appendix F.11.

rubrics_metrics.name: SNSF Proposal Evaluation Criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: External reviewers assess proposals against SNSF evaluation criteria: (1) Scientific relevance, originality and topicality, (2) Suitability of methods and feasibility, (3) Applicant’s scientific track record and expertise; plus (1a) Broader impact for 'use-inspired' proposals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the funder-facing criteria that reviewers are instructed to address in text boxes; the twelve annotation categories map to aspects of these SNSF criteria. The peer review reports analyzed contain up to five separate text comments addressing these criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentence-level annotation protocol
rubrics_metrics.description: Annotate single sentences for presence/absence of each of the twelve categories; categories are not mutually exclusive; Rationale only annotated if Positive or Negative is present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each sentence can have multiple category labels. Sentences were randomly sampled and assigned to three of four annotators. Aggregate annotations by majority agreement (≥2 of 3 annotators). Annotation rounds were iterative with codebook refinement across eleven rounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annotation sampling and dataset composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Annotated set comprised 3,000 sentences: first 2,000 sampled randomly from the English reviews; remaining 1,000 sentences stratified (200 from each of five SNSF text boxes). Full corpus: 47,522 external peer review reports for 13,653 applications; analysis limited to English reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stratified sampling was used to increase representation of under-represented categories (e.g., Applicant: Quantity). The corpus distribution across research domains: MINT 38.3%, Life Sciences 36.9%, SSH 24.7%.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annotation aggregation and inter-coder reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: Each sentence was annotated by three annotators and labels aggregated based on majority agreement; inter-coder agreement and disagreements were analyzed after each round to refine the codebook.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Majority-based consensus (≥2 of 3) reduces annotator bias. Agreement rates varied by category (64%–98%), average ~80%. The codebook and rounds ensured consistency; Appendix F lists full-agreement examples and Appendix D descriptive stats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training/test split and cross-validation protocol
rubrics_metrics.description: Annotated set split into training (2,500) and test (500) sentences; within training set, 5-fold stratified cross-validation was used (fine-tune on 4 folds, validate on 1), reporting average metrics across folds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stratification by outcome category used to preserve label distributions. For multi-label classification, stratification across labels was not feasible due to imbalance. Five-fold cross-validation ensures robustness against a single split.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification approach comparison and recommendation
rubrics_metrics.description: Three classification paradigms compared: binary (12 separate binary classifiers), multi-label (single model with 12 outputs), and multi-task (shared encoder with category-specific adapters).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical findings: separate binary classifiers performed best (average macro F1 ≈ 0.83–0.85), multi-label lower (≈0.71–0.73), multi-task worst (≈0.60–0.62). Trade-offs: binary is computationally intensive but robust to class imbalance; multi-label efficient but suffers from rare label combinations; multi-task reduces compute but may underfit category-specific patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transformer model choice and fine-tuning procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Use pre-trained transformer encoders (SPECTER2, BERT, RoBERTa) and fine-tune on annotated sentences; extract CLS token embeddings and add a linear output layer with sigmoid activation for binary prediction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SPECTER2 (pre-trained on scientific texts and citation graphs) was used and performed similarly to BERT and RoBERTa; annotated data quality mattered more than model choice. Fine-tuning details: AdamW optimizer, learning rate 2e-5, weight decay 0.01, 3 epochs, batch size 10; thresholding at 0.5 for binary predictions. Note GPU constraints (example: NVIDIA RTX A2000 4GB).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation metrics and reporting conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Report accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 score; compute micro-average and macro-average metrics and report class-specific metrics as well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preferred evaluation measure: macro-averaged F1 (weights labels equally, important under class imbalance). Micro-average dominated by prevalent classes. Also report class-specific precision/recall and consider balanced accuracy. Use repeated cross-validation averages for robust estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling class imbalance and prevalence effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Class label imbalance presents challenges: many categories are rare; prevalence correlates with classifier performance for multi-label and multi-task approaches but less so for binary classifiers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Binary classifiers were less affected by prevalence. For multi-label/multi-task, performance increased with label prevalence. Strategies include stratified sampling in annotation, separate binary modeling, and careful metric selection (macro F1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Explainability via keyness analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess face validity of classifiers by identifying terms and multi-word expressions that predict each category using keyness (chi-squared) tests and collocation analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply classifiers to the full corpus, compare sentences predicted present vs absent, compute chi-squared keyness for terms/phrases, and review top terms (Table 4 shows 25 top terms per category). Use results to validate model behavior qualitatively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data cleaning, anonymization, and language restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Clean raw texts by removing redundant characters, HTML code, and personal names; limit analysis to English reviews (non-English reviews excluded).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The dataset was anonymized to remove applicant/co-applicant/project partner names. 10.2% of reviews in other languages (mainly German and French) were excluded. Maintain a data management plan for privacy (DOI provided).

rubrics_metrics.name: LLM few-shot annotation experiments and conclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Test LLM few-shot classification (Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct) with prompts based on codebook examples to augment labeling or as direct classifier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Few-shot LLM performance was substantially worse (average macro F1 ≈ 0.70) than fine-tuned transformer classifiers (≈0.85), particularly on imbalanced categories. Recommendation: do not rely on LLM few-shot annotations or generated data for this task; fine-tune models on human-annotated domain data instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annotation aggregation threshold and training-set variants
rubrics_metrics.description: Primary aggregation rule: majority agreement (≥2 of 3) for labeling. Experiments also considered training only on sentences with full agreement (3 of 3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using only full-agreement sentences can change performance for some categories; Rationale annotation and other difficult categories may benefit from context or surrounding sentences. Report differences when limiting to full-agreement data (Appendix E.3 and A8).
